good_tf:
resource "azurerm_network_security_rule" "example" {
  name                        = "allow-ssh"
  priority                    = 100
  direction                   = "Inbound"
  access                      = "Allow"
  protocol                    = "Tcp"
  source_port_range           = "*"
  destination_port_range      = "22"
  source_address_prefix       = "10.0.0.0/24" # FIX: restrict SSH source to internal CIDR
  destination_address_prefix  = "*"
  resource_group_name         = "example-rg"
  network_security_group_name = "example-nsg"
}
why_it_matters: Exposing port 22 directly to the public internet allows unauthenticated attackers anywhere to discover and attempt authentication against SSH services on associated virtual machines.
Publicly accessible SSH daemons face continuous automated brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and potential exploitation of zero-day vulnerabilities in the SSH implementation.
Restricting source addresses to trusted private IP ranges or corporate jump hosts ensures that SSH endpoints cannot be probed or attacked directly from untrusted networks.
post_en:
Leaving SSH exposed to the public internet creates an immediate vector for automated brute-force attacks and remote server compromise.

Checkov check CKV_AZURE_10 flags Azure Network Security Group rules that permit inbound SSH traffic on port 22 from the public internet.

When an inbound NSG rule allows TCP traffic on destination port 22 with a source prefix set to any wildcard or internet tag, any host on the public internet can initiate a handshake with your virtual machines. Attackers continuously scan cloud IP spaces for listening SSH daemons to conduct automated credential stuffing, brute-force password guessing, and exploit unpatched software vulnerabilities. Once an attacker gains a foothold through an exposed port, they achieve interactive command execution within your network perimeter.

To resolve this misconfiguration, update the azurerm_network_security_rule resource by configuring source_address_prefix to a specific trusted CIDR block or private subnet such as 10.0.0.0/24 instead of a wildcard.

How do you currently verify that administrative management ports across your virtual networks are reachable only through bastion hosts or private corporate gateways?
